name: Mark
author: John Mark, companion of Peter and Paul
introduction:
The Gospel according to Mark begins with striking immediacy: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." Unlike the other Gospels, Mark omits any genealogy or birth story, thrusting readers directly into the public ministry of Jesus. He portrays Jesus as the mighty Son of God who arrives not to be served but to serve and to offer His life as a ransom for many. The narrative unfolds rapidly, with the term "immediately" occurring more than forty times, driving the story forward from one powerful event to another and conveying the unstoppable advance of God's kingdom breaking into human history through Jesus' words and actions.

Mark prioritizes Jesus' deeds over lengthy teachings, showcasing His divine authority through miraculous acts rather than extended sermons. In swift succession, Jesus expels demons, heals the sick, cleanses lepers, stills storms, feeds thousands, walks on water, and even raises the dead. These extraordinary acts reveal His divine power over sickness, evil spirits, nature, and death itself. Yet Jesus consistently orders silence about His true identity, a phenomenon scholars term the "messianic secret," deliberately avoiding public acclaim and rejecting political messianic hopes.

The pivotal moment of the Gospel occurs at Caesarea Philippi (8:27-30), where Peter declares Jesus to be "the Christ." From that point, the story turns resolutely toward Jerusalem and the cross. Jesus foretells His suffering and death three times (8:31; 9:31; 10:33-34), each prediction met with misunderstanding by His disciples and followed by teachings that true greatness is found in servanthood and suffering. The latter half of Mark reveals that this Son of God has come not to reign in visible glory immediately, but to suffer, die, and rise again. The cross stands at the center of Mark’s portrayal—Jesus is the Suffering Servant who triumphs through surrender and saves others by not saving Himself.

Mark’s Gospel culminates not with detailed resurrection appearances but with the empty tomb and the young man’s proclamation: "He is risen." The original ending (16:8) closes with the women fleeing in fear and trembling, compelling readers to wrestle with the Gospel’s central question: Will we, like the first followers, commit to this crucified and risen Lord? Will we take up our cross and follow Him? Thus, Mark offers not merely historical information about Jesus but a call to radical discipleship, inviting believers to walk the path of self-denial, sacrifice, and faithful witness to the Servant King.

key_themes.theme: Jesus as the Powerful Son of God
key_themes.description: Mark begins by declaring Jesus as the "Son of God" (1:1), a title affirmed by God’s voice at His baptism (1:11) and transfiguration (9:7), confessed by unclean spirits (3:11; 5:7), and finally acknowledged by the Roman centurion at the cross (15:39). Jesus exercises divine authority over demons, illness, nature, and death—domains belonging solely to God. His miraculous deeds reveal Him as the One who inaugurates God’s kingdom with sovereign power.

key_themes.theme: The Suffering Servant Who Gives His Life
key_themes.description: Though endowed with power, Jesus came "not to be served but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many" (10:45). The Gospel’s latter half focuses intently on the cross—Jesus’ suffering is intentional and redemptive. He is the Suffering Servant foretold by Isaiah who carries our sins. This paradox shapes Mark’s Christology: the mighty Son of God conquers through suffering and death.

Throughout Mark, Jesus repeatedly instructs silence regarding His identity—demons are forbidden to reveal Him, those healed are told to say nothing, and disciples are commanded not to declare Him Messiah. This "messianic secret" guards against political misunderstandings of His mission. Only after the cross can His true identity be fully grasped. Genuine knowledge of Jesus requires recognizing Him as the crucified Messiah, not merely a miracle worker.

key_themes.theme: Discipleship as Following the Crucified Christ
key_themes.description: Mark emphasizes costly discipleship: "Whoever wants to follow me must deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me" (8:34). True greatness is found in serving others (9:35; 10:43-44). To be Jesus’ disciple means embracing suffering rather than seeking worldly status or power. The disciples’ repeated failure to understand this offers both caution and encouragement—Jesus patiently instructs His imperfect followers.

Jesus proclaims that "the kingdom of God is near" (1:15), calling for repentance and faith. This kingdom arrives with power in Jesus’ person and works, yet remains partially hidden (4:11). Parables illustrate how the kingdom grows from small beginnings to universal reach, working secretly like a seed beneath the soil. The kingdom’s full revelation awaits the Son of Man’s glorious return (13:26; 14:62).

Mark contrasts faith and fear throughout his narrative. Jesus frequently asks, "Where is your faith?" (4:40) and encourages, "Do not fear, only believe" (5:36). Faith means trusting Jesus’ power and identity despite adverse circumstances. The disciples’ fears—of storms, Jesus’ identity, and the cross—gradually give way to faith. The Gospel challenges readers: Will we respond with fear or with trust?

key_themes.theme: The Failure and Restoration of the Disciples
key_themes.description: Mark presents the disciples’ shortcomings more starkly than other Gospels—they misunderstand Jesus’ mission, quarrel about status, sleep in Gethsemane, flee at His arrest, and Peter denies Him thrice. Yet Jesus remains patient, continually teaching them. The angel’s message to Peter (16:7) hints at restoration. This theme encourages all who struggle in faith—Jesus is gracious with imperfect followers.

Mark’s frequent use of "immediately" (Greek: euthys) creates a sense of pressing urgency. Events unfold swiftly; decisions require prompt response. When Jesus calls, disciples leave their nets "at once" (1:18). This urgency reflects the kingdom’s arrival and demands wholehearted commitment. The time is brief; the kingdom calls for immediate and total dedication.

key_verses.text: The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.
key_verses.significance: Mark's opening verse announces the Gospel's central thesis: Jesus is both the **Christ (Messiah)** and the **Son of God**. The entire narrative demonstrates and develops these two titles. The word **"gospel"** (good news) frames the book, appearing at the beginning (1:1), in Jesus' preaching (1:14-15), and in the call to discipleship (8:35; 10:29). This is not just information about Jesus but the saving message of God's kingdom breaking into history through His Son.

key_verses.text: The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.
key_verses.significance: Jesus' programmatic announcement summarizes His message. The **kingdom of God** has drawn near in His person and ministry. The proper response combines **repentance** (turning from sin and self-rule) and **faith** (trusting Jesus and His message). This verse establishes the urgency that pervades the Gospel—the decisive moment has arrived; immediate response is required.

key_verses.text: And he saith unto them, But whom say ye that I am? And Peter answereth and saith unto him, Thou art the Christ.
key_verses.significance: Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi marks the **dramatic center** of the Gospel. The question of Jesus' identity, implicit throughout the first half, receives explicit answer. Yet immediately Jesus begins teaching about His coming suffering (8:31), showing that 'Christ' must be understood in light of the cross, not popular messianic expectations of political power.

key_verses.text: And when he had called the people unto him with his disciples also, he said unto them, Whosoever will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. For whosoever will save his life shall lose it; but whosoever shall lose his life for my sake and the gospel's, the same shall save it.
key_verses.significance: Jesus defines **costly discipleship**. Following Him requires self-denial and cross-bearing—not mere moral improvement but death to self-centered life. The paradox is profound: **losing life to find it**. Attempts to preserve life through self-protection result in loss; surrendering life for Jesus and the gospel results in true life. This is the heart of Mark's call to discipleship.

key_verses.text: For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.
key_verses.significance: This verse summarizes Jesus' mission and provides the **theological center** of the Gospel. Despite His divine authority, Jesus came to serve, not to be served. His death is a **ransom**—the price paid to liberate slaves from bondage. The **"many"** for whom He gives His life anticipates the universal scope of redemption. This is Mark's clearest statement of substitutionary atonement.

key_verses.text: And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani? which is, being interpreted, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
key_verses.significance: Jesus' cry from the cross, quoting Psalm 22:1, expresses the **depth of His suffering**—not just physical agony but the horror of bearing sin and experiencing divine abandonment. The powerful Son of God, who commanded demons and calmed storms, now hangs helpless on a cross, enduring God-forsakenness to accomplish redemption. This is the nadir before the triumph of resurrection.

key_verses.text: And when the centurion, which stood over against him, saw that he so cried out, and gave up the ghost, he said, Truly this man was the Son of God.
key_verses.significance: A **Gentile centurion's confession** at the cross provides the climax of Mark's Christology. What demons knew from the beginning (1:24; 3:11; 5:7) and what Peter confessed halfway through (8:29), the centurion now declares watching Jesus die. Ironically, Jesus' identity as **Son of God** is most clearly revealed not in His miracles but in His death. The cross is God's power and wisdom.

outline.description: The ministry of John the Baptist, Jesus’ baptism, and His testing in the wilderness
Jesus calls His disciples, performs miracles, engages in disputes, and teaches in parables
Feeding the 5,000, walking on water, and feeding the 4,000
Peter’s confession of Christ, Jesus’ passion predictions, and instructions on discipleship
Triumphal entry into Jerusalem, cleansing of the temple, and the Olivet discourse
The Last Supper, Gethsemane, Jesus’ trial, crucifixion, and the empty tomb

historical_context:
The early church unanimously attributes the Gospel to John Mark, a close associate of both Peter and Paul. Papias, writing around AD 125, records that Mark acted as Peter’s interpreter in Rome, carefully recording Peter’s preaching about Jesus without necessarily following chronological order. This explains the Gospel’s vivid eyewitness details and its focus on Peter, including candid accounts of Peter’s failures. Mark appears in Acts (12:12, 25; 13:5, 13; 15:37-39) as the son of Mary, whose home hosted the Jerusalem church, as Barnabas’s cousin, and later as a companion of Paul (Colossians 4:10; 2 Timothy 4:11; Philemon 24).

The Gospel was likely composed in Rome between AD 55 and 65, possibly shortly before the temple’s destruction in AD 70 (the apocalyptic discourse in chapter 13 anticipates but does not describe this event). Internal evidence supports a Roman setting: Mark explains Jewish customs for Gentile readers (7:3-4; 14:12; 15:42), translates Aramaic expressions (3:17; 5:41; 7:11, 34; 15:22, 34), and uses Latin loanwords (4:21; 6:27; 12:14, 42; 15:16, 39). The emphasis on suffering and persecution fits the context of Nero’s persecution (AD 64-68), when Roman Christians faced martyrdom. Both Peter and Paul likely died during this period.

Mark’s primarily Gentile audience needed to grasp that following Jesus meant embracing suffering rather than expecting immediate political deliverance or comfort. The Gospel answers why the powerful Son of God suffered and died, and what that means for believers facing persecution. Mark portrays the cross not as defeat but as victory, true greatness as servanthood, and discipleship as following the path of the suffering Master. This Gospel provided theological foundation and encouragement for believers enduring trials and persecution.
literary_style:
Mark’s writing style is vivid, fast-moving, and focused on action. He frequently employs the present tense (the "historical present"), which creates immediacy and immerses readers in the scenes. Specific, tangible details suggest eyewitness testimony: the grass was green where the 5,000 sat (6:39), Jesus took Peter, James, and John with Him (5:37; 9:2; 14:33), and a young man fled naked, leaving his linen cloth behind (14:51-52). Emotional nuances appear throughout—Jesus looks around with anger (3:5), sighs deeply (8:12), is moved with compassion (6:34), and is greatly amazed (6:6).

The word "immediately" (Greek: euthys) occurs over forty times, generating relentless momentum. Events follow one another rapidly with minimal transition, underscoring the urgency of the kingdom’s arrival and the demand for prompt response. This feature makes Mark the most dramatic and urgent of the Gospels, sweeping the reader from one powerful episode to the next without pause.

The "messianic secret" motif—Jesus’ repeated commands to silence about His identity—creates ongoing narrative tension. Demons are forbidden to reveal Him (1:25, 34; 3:11-12), those healed must keep quiet (1:44; 5:43; 7:36; 8:26), and after Peter’s confession, the disciples are told not to proclaim His messiahship (8:30). Only after the resurrection is the secret to be disclosed (9:9). This theme prevents misunderstanding Jesus’ mission as a political revolt and shows that His identity can only be rightly understood in light of the cross.

Structurally, Mark’s Gospel centers on three passion predictions (8:31; 9:31; 10:33-34), each followed by the disciples’ lack of understanding and Jesus’ teaching on true discipleship (8:32-38; 9:33-37; 10:35-45). The Gospel naturally divides at Peter’s confession (8:29)—the first half highlights Jesus’ authority through mighty deeds, the second half reveals His mission to suffer and die. Geographically, the narrative moves from Galilee (chapters 1-9) to Jerusalem (chapters 10-16), shifting from proclamation to passion.

The Gospel’s ending has been debated throughout church history. The earliest and most reliable manuscripts conclude at 16:8 with the women fleeing the empty tomb in fear and silence. This abrupt ending (ending with the Greek word gar, "for") may be an intentional literary device by Mark, leaving readers to decide whether they will follow the risen Lord. Later manuscripts include a longer ending (16:9-20) with resurrection appearances and the Great Commission, likely added by scribes to complete the narrative.
theological_significance:
Mark’s Gospel offers distinctive theological insights while sharing foundational apostolic teaching with the other Gospels. Its Christology presents Jesus as the powerful Son of God who willingly embraces the path of suffering service. The title "Son of God" frames the Gospel (1:1, though textually debated; 15:39), receives divine affirmation (1:11; 9:7), and is confessed by demons (3:11; 5:7). Jesus exercises divine prerogatives such as forgiving sins (2:5-7), accepting worship (5:6), and asserting authority over the Sabbath (2:28). His mighty works demonstrate power that belongs solely to God: dominion over demons, disease, nature, and death.

Yet this divine Son came "not to be served but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many" (10:45). Mark’s theology of the cross is central: Jesus’ suffering is purposeful, not accidental. The term "ransom" (lytron) signifies substitutionary payment—Jesus’ life is given in exchange for many, freeing them from sin and death’s bondage. The cup Jesus drinks (10:38-39; 14:36) symbolizes God’s wrath against sin (cf. Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17). His death accomplishes what the sacrificial system foreshadowed—atonement for sin.

Mark’s teaching on discipleship is demanding and realistic. Following Jesus requires self-denial, cross-bearing, and losing one’s life (8:34-35)—not mere moral improvement but dying to self-rule. True greatness comes through serving others (9:35; 10:43-44), the last become first (9:35; 10:31), and suffering leads to glory (10:38-40). The disciples’ persistent failures—their misunderstanding, ambition, fear, and abandonment—highlight the difficulty of discipleship and Jesus’ patience with imperfect followers. Mark offers no idealized portrait of following Christ.

Regarding eschatology, Mark presents the kingdom as both present and future. The kingdom of God draws near in Jesus (1:15), breaking into history with power. Yet its full revelation awaits the Son of Man’s glorious return (8:38; 13:26; 14:62), an event that will come "with power" (9:1) within the lifetime of some standing with Jesus. The apocalyptic discourse (chapter 13) warns of coming tribulation, calls for watchfulness, and promises the gathering of the elect. The kingdom’s present hiddenness and future glory create the tension in which disciples live.

Mark’s pneumatology highlights the Spirit’s role in Jesus’ ministry. The Spirit descends at Jesus’ baptism (1:10), empowering His work. The Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness to be tempted (1:12). Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit—attributing Jesus’ Spirit-empowered deeds to Satan—is the unforgivable sin (3:28-29). The Spirit will empower disciples’ witness amid persecution (13:11). Though less developed than Luke’s pneumatology, Mark establishes the Spirit’s essential role in Jesus’ mission and the disciples’ testimony.
christ_in_book:
Mark portrays Jesus wearing two contrasting crowns: one of divine authority and one of suffering service. From the outset, Jesus is introduced as "the Christ, the Son of God" (1:1)—titles that the entire Gospel unfolds. He is the Son of God confirmed by the Father’s voice at His baptism (1:11) and transfiguration (9:7), reluctantly acknowledged by demons throughout His ministry (1:24; 3:11; 5:7), and confessed by the Gentile centurion at the cross (15:39). This sonship is not symbolic but ontological—Jesus possesses God’s nature, authority, and prerogatives.

Jesus’ mighty works demonstrate His divine authority and identity. He commands demons, and they obey (1:25-27); He heals incurable diseases—leprosy, paralysis, hemorrhage (1:40-45; 2:1-12; 5:25-34); He calms storms that terrify His disciples, prompting them to ask, "What kind of man is this, that even the wind and sea obey Him?" (4:41); He walks on water (6:48), declaring "It is I" (ego eimi)—possibly alluding to God’s self-revelation in the Old Testament; He feeds thousands with a few loaves and fish (6:30-44; 8:1-10); He raises the dead (5:21-43). These signs reveal Him as the One who brings God’s kingdom with power.

Mark’s unique contribution is showing how this powerful Son of God is also the Suffering Servant. The turning point comes at Caesarea Philippi when Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ (8:29), and Jesus immediately begins teaching about His coming suffering, rejection, death, and resurrection (8:31). This pattern repeats with three passion predictions (8:31; 9:31; 10:33-34), each met with the disciples’ confusion and followed by instruction that true greatness comes through servanthood and suffering. Jesus "came not to be served but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many" (10:45).

Mark also identifies Jesus as the Son of Man—a title combining heavenly glory (Daniel 7:13-14) with earthly suffering (Isaiah 53). As Son of Man, Jesus has authority to forgive sins (2:10) and lordship over the Sabbath (2:28), yet He must suffer, be rejected, and die (8:31; 9:31; 10:33-34). The Son of Man will return "in the clouds with great power and glory" (13:26) to gather His elect and judge the world (8:38). This title unites Jesus’ present humiliation with His future exaltation.

The cross is Mark’s theological and narrative climax. The mighty Son of God who cast out demons and raised the dead now hangs powerless, mocked by those He came to save. His cry of abandonment—"My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?" (15:34)—expresses genuine separation as He bears the penalty of sin. Yet even in death, Jesus displays authority: the temple veil tears from top to bottom (God’s act, 15:38), and the centurion confesses, "Truly this man was the Son of God" (15:39). Mark shows the cross as victory, not defeat; power, not weakness; the fullest revelation of Jesus’ sonship.

The resurrection vindicates Jesus and reverses the cross’s apparent defeat. The empty tomb, the angel’s announcement ("He is risen," 16:6), and the promise that Jesus goes before His disciples to Galilee confirm His predictions. Whether Mark’s Gospel originally ended at 16:8 or included additional material, the resurrection is proclaimed and Jesus’ triumph established. He is the crucified and risen Lord who calls disciples to follow Him on the path of the cross, promising that those who lose their lives for His sake and the gospel’s will save them (8:35).
relationship_to_new_testament:
Mark’s Gospel is widely regarded as the earliest of the four canonical Gospels, likely serving as a primary source for Matthew and Luke (the "Markan priority" hypothesis accepted by most scholars). About 90% of Mark’s content appears in Matthew, and roughly 50% in Luke, though both include additional material from other sources (including the hypothetical "Q" and their unique traditions). Mark’s vivid, action-driven narrative provides the foundational framework adapted by the other synoptic evangelists for their distinct audiences and purposes.

Mark’s connection to Peter’s preaching explains much of its content and perspective. Early church fathers such as Papias, Irenaeus, and Clement of Alexandria unanimously attest that Mark recorded Peter’s teachings. Peter’s prominence in the Gospel—his call, confession, rebuke, denial, and the angel’s specific mention of him in 16:7—supports this tradition. The epistle 1 Peter 5:13 may reference Mark: "Marcus my son" greets the churches, indicating close association between Peter and Mark in Rome.

The Gospel’s pneumatology and eschatology align with broader New Testament teaching. The Spirit’s descent on Jesus at His baptism (1:10) sets the pattern for Spirit-empowered ministry described in Acts (chapter 2). The warning against blasphemy of the Holy Spirit (3:28-29) echoes similar admonitions in Matthew (12:31-32), Luke (12:10), and Hebrews (6:4-6). The apocalyptic discourse (Mark 13) provides essential background for understanding Pauline eschatology (1-2 Thessalonians), Peter’s warnings (1-2 Peter), and Revelation.

Mark’s emphasis on suffering discipleship informs New Testament theology of following Christ. Paul’s teaching on union with Christ in His death and resurrection (Romans 6:1-11; Galatians 2:20; Philippians 3:10-11) develops the narrative Mark presents—following Jesus means dying to self to share His resurrected life. Hebrews’ portrayal of Jesus as the pioneer of salvation perfected through suffering (Hebrews 2:10; 5:8-9) echoes Mark’s suffering Son of God.

Mark’s servant Christology significantly influences New Testament ecclesiology and ethics. Jesus’ declaration that "the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve" (10:45) becomes the model for church leadership (1 Peter 5:1-5) and mutual service (Galatians 5:13; Philippians 2:3-8). Paul’s self-identification as a "servant of Jesus Christ" (Romans 1:1) and his call to have Christ’s humility (Philippians 2:5-11) flow from Jesus’ example in Mark.

Mark’s ransom theology (10:45) provides key vocabulary for New Testament soteriology. The concept of Jesus’ death as ransom (lytron) appears in Paul (1 Timothy 2:6—antilytron, "ransom for all"; Titus 2:14—lytroo, "redeem") and Peter (1 Peter 1:18-19—lytroo, redeemed with precious blood). This ransom accomplishes what Old Testament redemption foreshadowed, liberating God’s people from sin and death through the blood of God’s own Son.
practical_application:
Mark challenges comfortable Christianity with the demanding call of discipleship. Jesus’ invitation remains clear and uncompromising: "Whoever wants to follow me must deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me" (8:34). This is not a call to occasional inconvenience but to death—death to self-rule, self-promotion, and self-preservation. The cross is not a metaphor for mild hardship but an instrument of execution. Yet this summons comes from the One who Himself bore the cross, lived what He taught, and gave His life as a ransom. We follow a crucified Savior on a cruciform path.

The Gospel’s honest portrayal of the disciples’ failures offers both warning and hope. Peter, James, and John—the inner circle—repeatedly misunderstand Jesus’ mission, quarrel over status, sleep when called to watch, and ultimately flee. Peter denies Jesus three times. Yet Jesus remains patient, continues teaching, and sends a specific message to Peter after the resurrection (16:7). This shows that Jesus works with imperfect followers, that stumbling does not disqualify us, and that restoration follows repentance. We need not pretend perfect discipleship; we must simply keep following.

Mark confronts the human desire for greatness and recognition that permeates religious communities. The disciples argue about who is greatest; James and John seek positions of honor; all desire acclaim. Jesus consistently replies, "If anyone wants to be first, he must be last of all and servant of all" (9:35). "Whoever wants to be chief must be servant of all" (10:44). True greatness is found in servanthood, not self-exaltation. Leadership means surrendering privilege to serve others, following Jesus’ example of ministering rather than being served.

The Gospel’s urgency calls for immediate, decisive response. When Jesus calls, fishermen leave their nets "at once" (1:18); Levi abandons his tax booth "and follows Him" (2:14). The kingdom has come; the time is fulfilled; delay is perilous. This confronts procrastination and half-hearted commitment. Following Jesus requires forsaking other loyalties—family, possessions, safety, status—and embracing His lordship fully. Mark’s rapid style reflects the kingdom’s urgent demands.

Mark teaches that faith must overcome fear. The disciples fear the storm until Jesus calms it; they fear when Jesus walks on water; they fear at His transfiguration; they fear His passion predictions; the women fear at the empty tomb. Jesus repeatedly challenges this fear: "Why are you so afraid? Have you no faith?" (4:40). "Do not be afraid; only believe" (5:36). Faith trusts Jesus’ power and person despite circumstances. Faith clings to His promises even when the future looks bleak. Faith follows the path through suffering to glory.

The messianic secret teaches that true understanding of Jesus requires recognizing Him as the crucified Messiah, not merely a miracle worker. We are tempted to desire Jesus’ benefits without His cross, His power without His suffering, His kingdom without His demands. But there is no crown without a cross, no resurrection without death, no glory without humiliation. We must embrace the whole Christ—mighty Son of God and suffering Servant—and follow Him on the full path He walked.

Finally, Mark calls believers to bold witness despite opposition and cost. The Gospel likely addresses Christians suffering under Nero’s persecution in Rome. The message is clear: follow Jesus faithfully even unto death. The Son of God obeyed the Father’s will though it led to the cross. He calls us to the same faithfulness. Our task is not self-preservation but to lose our lives for His sake and the gospel’s, trusting that those who lose their lives will save them (8:35). The gospel must be preached to all nations (13:10), and we are Christ’s witnesses "to the ends of the earth," empowered by His presence and assured of final victory when the Son of Man returns in glory.
